name: Agent Hardening Sprint
one_liner: Fixed-fee red team of a small company's coding agents, MCP servers and CI agent jobs, then hardening through vendor-native managed settings, sandboxing and tested guardrails.
entry_price: $6,500 fixed fee for up to 25 developers and 3 CI repositories (2-week sprint: inventory, red team, CI hardening, native-control setup, re-test); quarterly re-test $1,800; partners buy at $5,000
majors: market-skeptic

The whole concept now rests on the trigger, and no evidence shows that it exists. The buyer is a CTO with a written customer-questionnaire item, auditor question or near-miss about coding agents. Published AI vendor questionnaire guidance (Vanta, GRC templates) asks about training on customer data, prompt retention, sub-processors and shadow AI. It does not ask for adversarial testing of developers' agents, MCP permissions or CI agent jobs. The concept cites no questionnaire, auditor or customer that asks for this. SOC 2 has no AI criteria (CSA). Without such a document, a red team is a discretionary $6,500.
market-skeptic

The problem evidence still comes from developers and tool authors. The new items (headless MCP auto-approval, an MCP read-only bypass, a missing subagent validator) are bugs in agent and MCP projects, reported by their own maintainers or users. They show that the risk is technically real. They do not show that a small-company CTO will pay an outsider to find it. None of them involves a target-profile company that was harmed, or one that asked for help.
competitor-analyst

Most dangerous competitor is still Vanta, and the threat now hits the core. Vanta's Pillar roadmap lists AI inventory and runtime monitoring for January 2027, red teaming ('adversarial testing tailored to your business context') for Spring 2027 and runtime enforcement for Summer 2027, sold inside the SOC 2 platform the named co-buyer already pays for. Pillar's catalogue includes coding agents and MCP servers. The concept's strongest claim, red teaming that platforms do not bundle, has a public expiry date. The implementation-partner role also depends on a Vanta partner track for AI services, and none has been published.
competitor-analyst

The claimed asset, a private injection suite of 30+ cases, is being commoditised. Promptfoo ships free, open coding-agent red-team plugins for repo-text injection, terminal-output injection, secret env and file reads, sandbox read and write escape, network egress bypass, delayed CI exfiltration and automation poisoning, run against an isolated repo copy. That is most of the concept's suite and test method. GitInject (live GitHub workflow injection) and SuperClaw add open tooling. An in-house platform engineer, or any pentest firm, can run this, so the work shifts from owning a suite to delivery and judgment.
competitor-analyst

The concept understates the boutique overlap. Its table says Appsecco 'tests MCP servers', but Appsecco sells fixed-price product security testing for agent workflows, MCP tools and connected data sources, with a 48-hour quote and a retest within 30 days. That is the same fixed-fee, retest-included structure, from a firm with published research and a client base. The differentiation from Christian Schneider holds, since his offer is an interview-based assessment and explicitly 'not a pentest'.
security-practitioner

The hardening leans on the native sandbox with an egress allowlist, but Claude Code's sandbox covers shell commands only. File tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it. The concept's headline exposure is MCP servers wired to GitHub, cloud and production data, so a poisoned issue that makes the agent call a write-capable MCP tool is not contained by the sandbox. MCP risk has to be cut at the server: an allowlist (allowedMcpServers/managed-mcp.json), per-tool deny rules, least-privilege tokens for each MCP server, and read-only database roles. None of these is named as a deliverable.
technical-feasibility

The new containment layer does not cover the main attack surface. Claude Code's sandbox covers shell commands only. Local MCP servers, hooks and the built-in file and web tools run outside it with full user access, and allowedDomains does not limit WebFetch. A poisoned issue that drives an MCP tool such as GitHub, a database or mail is limited only by the MCP allowlist, permission rules and token scope, not by the sandbox or the egress allowlist. The hardening must add per-server least-privilege tokens, deny rules on MCP write tools and possibly containerised MCP servers. The bypass list must say plainly that the sandbox does not cover MCP.
gtm-pricing

Demand still depends on a trigger and has no budget line. Narrowing the buyer to companies with a written questionnaire item, an auditor question or a near-miss is honest, but it shrinks the funnel to a segment nobody has sized. It also makes deal flow follow the slow, uneven questionnaire cycle. No evidence yet shows partners or CTOs actually have such requests in hand.
gtm-pricing

Two sprints a month is optimistic for one person who must also write 2-3 public research pieces, keep a 30+ case injection suite current across four agents, run free self-scan walkthroughs, manage partners and handle engagement paperwork. Early utilisation is more likely 1-1.5 sprints a month, so $6.5-10k gross before insurance and partner discounts. First revenue is expected around month 3-5, so year one may bring in well under $100k.
legal-ethics

The red team runs on 'a fork of a real repo' with the client's real MCP server versions in a disposable environment. Unless that environment runs in the client's own cloud account, with the client's own agent licences, the founder now holds the client's private source code. Every injection run also sends that code to an LLM provider under the founder's API account and data terms, not the client's. This contradicts the claim that 'the founder never holds client data'. It also makes the founder a sub-processor that the client's SOC 2 vendor review and its customers' DPAs have to cover. The concept needs a custody design before the first sprint. The default should be an environment in the client's tenant, using the client's agent accounts, destroyed at the end of the sprint with written confirmation. Otherwise it needs a DPA, a named LLM provider with zero-retention terms, encryption, and deletion on close.
legal-ethics

The liability controls are listed but not yet contracted or priced. 'Production credentials only with written approval' leaves a door open that a client under deadline pressure will push through, and a successful injection with a production token can delete or exfiltrate data. E&O and cyber cover for a new solo firm doing offensive testing remains an open question. The rationale says the price 'covers insurance', but gives no quote. Before selling, the founder needs three things: a signed engagement template with an authorisation letter, a third-party exclusion and a liability cap at or near the fee; a written rule that production testing uses read-only or single-resource tokens and has a rollback plan; and a bound policy.
economic-buyer

The new price puts the sprint head-to-head with the security spend I already have. $6,500 is about what a small SaaS pays for its whole annual pentest: fixed-price vendors quote $4,000 for web app and API plus $2,400 for cloud, $6,400 in total. That pentest is what customers and SOC 2 auditors actually ask for. At $3,500 I could put it on a card; at $6,500 it needs a budget conversation, and the CFO will ask why a coding-agent test costs as much as the test of our product. Without a written trigger, I defer it to next year's budget.
economic-buyer

The must-have trigger is still an assumption, not evidence. The revision narrows the buyer to companies with a written questionnaire item or auditor question about coding agents, but the concept shows none. The enterprise AI questionnaires I can find ask about the vendor's AI product (model behaviour, refusals, retention, training, guardrails), not about how its developers configure Claude Code or MCP. The concept itself says SOC 2 has no AI criteria. The segment that has a real trigger may be very small.
defensibility

The 'private, growing injection-test suite' the differentiation names as the asset is already free and maintained. Promptfoo's coding-agent collection covers repo prompt injection, terminal-output injection, secret env/file reads, sandbox read/write escape, egress bypass, delayed CI exfil, automation poisoning and verifier sabotage, with MCP plugins and disposable-checkout guidance. That is a superset of the planned 30+ cases, backed by a vendor that is part of OpenAI.
defensibility

The likeliest copier is still the small pentest, vCISO and SOC 2 readiness firm, now invited in as a reseller. Wholesale resale at $5,000 is not exclusive and teaches the method: after a few sprints a partner can run Promptfoo plus native managed settings itself and keep the whole $6,500. Established boutiques that already sell coding-agent or MCP assessments (listed in competitors) can add a fixed price within a quarter.
defensibility

There are no switching costs. Fixes live in the client's native managed settings, sandbox config and log store by design, and the quarterly re-test ($1,800) can go to any tester. Compliance platforms (Vanta, Drata) that own the buyer relationship could add an automated red-team check or a partner service and pull re-tests away.
founder-fit

Credibility is still unproven and everything depends on it. The plan now puts 2-3 write-ups before selling, but the direct and partner channels both need the founder to look like a coding-agent security expert. Established boutiques already publish deep coding-agent work, such as Christian Schneider's ten-domain assessment and cheat sheet. Pentest and vCISO firms will not resell an unknown solo tester's red team until they see a finding or a reference client.
founder-fit

Time to first revenue is long for a founder with no capital. The plan needs 3 months to build the test environment, the 30+ case suite and the write-ups, plus about a month to learn agent managed settings, sandbox and hook semantics, GitHub Actions attack paths and SOC 2 control wording. With the 2-week test after that and a typical first-deal cycle, the first $6,500 arrives around month 4-6. The founder has plenty of time, so this is survivable but not fast. A paid one-repository CI test could close earlier.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: Enough 15-150 person SaaS companies have a concrete trigger (a customer questionnaire item, auditor question or near-miss about coding agents) to pay about $6,500 for a red team and hardening now, directly or through a partner firm.
riskiest_assumption.test: In two weeks: interview 10 SOC 2 readiness, vCISO or small pentest firms about how often clients get coding-agent or MCP questions and offer them the wholesale sprint; contact 20 CTOs from the founder's network and research readers, ask whether they have such a request in writing, and offer a pre-sold sprint with a $1,000 deposit.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: At least 3 of 10 partner firms report clients with written coding-agent questions and 2 agree in writing to refer or resell, and at least 1 CTO pays a deposit at $6,500 (or 2 at the one-repository CI test).

change_my_mind: market-skeptic
3 of 10 SOC 2 readiness, vCISO or pentest firms show redacted client questionnaires or audit requests that ask about coding-agent, MCP or CI-agent controls
competitor-analyst
Vanta/Pillar red teaming ships for AI apps only, or at enterprise tiers only, and leaves developer coding agents and CI agent jobs out of scope through 2027
security-practitioner

MCP-specific hardening added as a deliverable: allowlist plus per-server least-privilege tokens or read-only roles, and a re-test showing a poisoned issue can no longer trigger a write-capable MCP tool.
technical-feasibility
A pilot client where an MCP-driven injection case (poisoned issue to a GitHub or database MCP write) is blocked by token scope or deny rules, not only shell cases by the sandbox.
gtm-pricing
At least 3 of 10 interviewed SOC 2 readiness, vCISO or pentest firms show client questionnaires with coding-agent or MCP items, and 2 sign a resale agreement at $5,000 wholesale
legal-ethics
A custody design where the disposable test environment runs in the client's tenant with the client's agent accounts, or a signed DPA with named zero-retention LLM terms and deletion on close.
economic-buyer
3 of 10 partner firms show redacted client questionnaires or auditor requests that name coding agents, MCP or CI agent jobs.
defensibility
Within 6 months, 2 or more vendor-acknowledged findings or CVEs in coding agents or popular MCP servers published under the founder's name
founder-fit
Within 3 months, 2-3 public reproducible coding-agent or CI-agent injection write-ups, at least one acknowledged by a vendor or maintainer, plus a talk accepted at a BSides or similar event.

name: Safeguards Desk
one_liner: Verified FTC Safeguards program for small tax, mortgage and accounting offices: read-only Microsoft 365 checks, required scans and tests, and evidence from real configuration.
entry_price: Program tier (firms with 5,000+ consumers): $490 setup + $179/month billed annually, up to 20 users, including continuous M365 checks, two external scans, one annual pen test, a tabletop and the annual report. Core tier (under 5,000): $39/month, monitor and WISP only.
majors: market-skeptic

The new wedge rests on a segment nobody has sized. We don't know how many 3-20 person tax, CPA and mortgage offices hold data on 5,000+ consumers, or whether they know it. Sources disagree on how to count consumers (active versus all retained records), so many owners will self-classify under the line and buy the $39 Core tier or the free IRS template. The concept lists this as its first open question. Without a count, the 40-client target can't be judged against the size of the market.
market-skeptic

Under 314.4(d)(2), the annual pen test and six-monthly scans are needed only 'absent effective continuous monitoring'. SBTPG/Watch Cloud already sells MDR plus 'Microsoft 365 & Google Workspace monitoring' through the tax-pro channel, and MSPs will say their RMM/EDR stack is continuous monitoring. Many firms above 5,000 consumers will reasonably believe they already meet the testing duty, which shrinks the market that is legally forced to buy. The concept's own continuous M365 monitor also blurs the line.
market-skeptic

The demand evidence still does not come from the named buyer. problem.evidence is regulation text plus old HN, ServerFault and StackExchange posts from tech-adjacent small firms. No tax-office, CPA or mortgage-broker owner or MSP asks for verification or testing. The revision log admits the problem was not changed. The pain is mandated on paper, but there is no evidence it is felt or budgeted.
market-skeptic

The levers that turn a duty into budget are weak for this segment. FTC enforcement against sub-20-person firms is rare. Industry guides to cyber-insurance requirements (seen only in search results, not opened) say small-firm applications gate on MFA, EDR and backups, and treat pen-test or scan summaries as optional evidence asked for at higher limits. Owners already pay $999 for a WISP plus $297-$697 for insurance, and have little outside pressure to add about $2,150 a year.
competitor-analyst

The most dangerous competitor is now Kaseya, with the MSP stack around it. The concept's channel is MSPs 'that lack security-testing staff', but those MSPs don't need staff: Kaseya's vPenTest runs automated internal and external pen tests monthly or on demand and is pitched as producing compliance-ready reports. ConnectSecure sells scheduled vulnerability scanning plus compliance reporting to MSPs 'in highly regulated industries'. An MSP that owns these tools can deliver 314.4(d)(2) evidence itself and keep the margin. It has no reason to resell a solo founder's manual test at 30% off. Kaseya also owns Compliance Manager GRC, so a Safeguards template on top is a short step.
competitor-analyst

The read-only M365 posture monitor, the concept's core feature, is commodity in the MSP channel. Microsoft 365 Lighthouse gives CSP partners SMB security baselines and multi-tenant risk views at no extra cost. CIPP (open source, built for MSPs) does multi-tenant standards and compliance reporting. Maester runs 2,000+ read-only checks against CIS/CISA baselines for free. The MFA, leaver, forwarding-rule and admin-role checks in the MVP are a subset of what partners already run. What's left to differentiate is the mapping to Safeguards sections and the report wording, not the detection.
competitor-analyst

Cynomi already sells an FTC Safeguards vCISO platform to MSPs and MSSPs. It automates risk assessments, program documentation and compliance reporting, and names mortgage brokers, tax preparers and accounting firms as targets. That is the partner console, tailored-WISP and risk-assessment layer of this MVP. It is already funded and already in the MSP channel. With Cynomi plus vPenTest, an MSP gets the whole Program tier from existing vendors.
competitor-analyst

Vertical WISP SaaS has moved toward 'continuous'. SafeGuardGRC/Kompflow sells a firm-specific WISP aligned with FTC 314 and Pub 4557 for $499 the first year, then $99/year, with auto-updates. Its higher tiers advertise a risk assessment, IR playbooks, vendor inventory, insurer questionnaires and 'continuous control testing'. The Core tier at $39/month (~$470/yr) is about 5x that price, and a WISP 'regenerated from findings' will not stay unique.
security-practitioner

The monitor reports by monthly email, but the signals it collects are attacks in progress. An external forwarding rule, a new Global Admin or a risky sign-in means business email compromise is happening now. Learning about it up to 30 days later is post-mortem evidence, not detection. On Entra ID Free tenants (Business Basic/Standard), sign-in and audit logs are kept for only 7 days, so a monthly pull misses most activity unless the product polls daily and stores the data. It needs near-real-time alerts to the owner and MSP for high-severity changes, and daily collection, or it does not reduce BEC risk or meaningfully address 314.4(c)(8) user-activity monitoring.
security-practitioner

The penetration test covers only 'internet-facing services and the M365 tenant', within a budget of about 8 founder hours per client per year that must also cover two scans, a tabletop and the report. Small tax and mortgage offices usually expose almost nothing externally. Their real compromise paths are phishing, infostealers or remote-access tools on workstations, shared local admin accounts, and tax or LOS software on office PCs. A test that never touches endpoints or the internal network produces a clean dated report while the main attack surface goes untested. That is checkbox compliance, the problem round 1 flagged in a new form, and an incident on an untested workstation would expose it.
security-practitioner

The checks the concept lists need tenant-wide application permissions: AuditLog.Read.All for sign-ins, MailboxSettings.Read for inbox rules on every mailbox, Policy/Directory reads, and app-only Exchange Online access for forwarding. These permissions stay granted indefinitely across dozens of financial firms' tenants. One stolen app secret or certificate, or a compromise of the founder's laptop, becomes a read path into every client and a ready map of their weaknesses (the findings database). Attackers have abused OAuth apps this way before. A solo founder running the platform with no 24/7 coverage is a concentrated supply-chain risk. MSPs and the 314.4(f) oversight duty will ask for evidence the concept does not yet plan: certificate auth held in an HSM or Key Vault, per-tenant app registrations or GDAP, Conditional Access for workload identities, an independent assessment, and a breach notification commitment.
technical-feasibility

Holding admin-consented application permissions (AuditLog.Read.All, Directory/Policy read, MailboxSettings read, Exchange.ManageAsApp) for dozens of financial-firm tenants makes one app secret or certificate a key to all of them. Read-only scopes still expose inbox rules, sign-in logs and the full user directory, which is exactly the reconnaissance a BEC attacker wants. The revision names vendor security as a hardest part but does not design it: certificate-only credentials in an HSM or Key Vault, per-tenant token isolation, no standing human access, and a 314.4(f)-ready security program. A solo founder has to build this to production quality inside the same three months.
technical-feasibility

Graph does not expose external forwarding settings (mailbox ForwardingSmtpAddress, remote-domain auto-forward, outbound spam policy). These need Exchange Online PowerShell app-only access, which requires Exchange.ManageAsApp plus a Microsoft Entra directory role assigned to the app's service principal in each client tenant, with certificate authentication and a PowerShell runtime in the backend. That is a per-tenant onboarding step beyond one-click admin consent, and small-office owners or wary MSPs may refuse it. It also complicates a Python/Graph-only backend.
technical-feasibility

Signal coverage varies by licence. Risky users and risk detections need Entra ID P2, which few 3-20-seat offices have. Sign-in log and registration-detail reports are tied to premium tiers, so they may be missing on Business Basic or Standard tenants. MFA coverage then has to fall back to per-user authentication-method enumeration and a check on security defaults or conditional access. The concept names this risk, but the MVP needs a per-SKU check matrix and test tenants for each SKU before launch, or the monthly evidence quietly varies by client.
technical-feasibility

Founder hours are underestimated. An annual pen test of external services plus an M365 tenant (scoping, written authorization, testing, retest, report), two scans with triage, a tabletop and an annual report will not fit in about 8 hours per client unless the test is a templated tool run. A templated run risks not counting as 'penetration testing' under 314.4(d)(2). At a realistic 15-25 hours, 40 clients needs 600-1,000 hours a year beside running the platform.
gtm-pricing

The go-to-market now depends on MSP resale: half of the first ten customers and the core channel. But the concept's own risks say MSPs may treat findings about their clients' tenants as a threat. A 30% margin on $179/month is about $54/month per office, a small incentive against the reputational risk of a third party grading their work. Many MSPs also already run their own scanning or compliance tooling. There is no MSP letter of intent, no partner economics and no CAC or payback figure for either channel.
gtm-pricing

Willingness to pay at $2.1k is unproven. The buyer's reference spend is a $999 Verito WISP plus $297-$697 insurance, and the concept itself flags low FTC enforcement and possible unawareness of the 5,000-consumer duty. Program costs $2,638 in year one with setup, roughly double the current spend. Unless an insurer questionnaire or examiner asks for test evidence, owners may keep the document plus insurance.
legal-ethics

Testing authorization does not cover third-party assets. Many target offices run tax or loan software on hosted desktops (Verito and ACE, which the concept lists as competitors, are hosting providers), on MSP-managed firewalls or on ISP-owned gear. A signature from the office owner does not authorize testing infrastructure the office does not own. Without the host's written consent, the test risks unauthorized access under the CFAA and state laws and breaches the host's terms. Microsoft's Rules of Engagement also bind the owner's authorized agents. They prohibit post-exploit actions, lateral movement, phishing through Microsoft services, DoS and the use of credentials other than your own. The M365 'pen test' therefore has to be scoped as configuration review plus limited testing, not as an attack simulation.
legal-ethics

The liability and insurance fix is still only a plan. The concept now adds active testing against production systems at financial offices. An outage or lockout during filing season, a missed critical finding later exploited, or a report a regulator rejects as (d)(2) evidence (open_questions[3]) could each lead to a claim. No E&O/cyber quote, liability cap or reviewed engagement terms exist yet, and the founder carries all of it personally.
economic-buyer

The wedge duty has a cheaper exit. 314.4(d)(2) requires annual pen tests and six-monthly vulnerability assessments only 'absent effective continuous monitoring'. If I already pay an MSP or a bundle such as SBTPG/Watch Cloud for 24x7 MDR, my IT provider will tell me that is continuous monitoring and the test is optional. So for many target firms the must-have becomes a nice-to-have, and I would not cut anything to fund it.
economic-buyer

Still no fear trigger I can show my CFO. No audit asks for the test, the concept itself lists FTC/state enforcement against sub-20-person firms and insurer questionnaires as open questions, and the 5,000-consumer count is my own estimate. A cost-conscious owner can count conservatively, file under the 314.6 exemption and keep the free template. The duty is real, but nothing makes me prove it.
economic-buyer

The price roughly doubles my current spend with no budget line to take it from. Year one is $490 + $2,148 = $2,638, against today's $999 Verito WISP or a free template plus $297-697 insurance. Being cheaper than a $3k-15k standalone pen test does not help: I never budgeted for a pen test, so I compare against what I pay now, not against an engagement I never bought.
defensibility

The most likely copier is now the partner channel itself. MSPs serving these offices can already put together the same Program from tools they have or get free. Microsoft 365 Lighthouse (no extra cost for CSP partners) offers an SMB security baseline, MFA adoption and risky sign-ins across tenants. Open-source CIPP checks tenant standards every 12 hours and reports, alerts on or fixes drift. ConnectSecure runs scheduled internal and external scans with white-label compliance reports. Kaseya vPenTest runs scheduled internal and external pen tests with auto-generated reports, which users call CREST-approved tests for SMB clients. Mapping that output to 314.4(d)(2) and a WISP is a template job. A partner-first plan teaches MSPs the playbook and then loses them.
defensibility

The M365 posture monitor, now the core feature, is commodity. Its checks are MFA coverage, leavers, forwarding rules, admin roles and risky sign-ins. Lighthouse covers MFA and risky sign-ins with SMB baselines for free, and CIPP covers drift for free. The monitor has no proprietary data and no network effect, and a single admin-consented Graph app is the same access every MSP tool uses.
defensibility

The bundlers with distribution can add the wedge in a quarter. SBTPG/Watch Cloud already sells a WISP, MDR and advisor briefings, billed from refund-transfer fees, and Verito already sells recurring WISPs. Either can add an automated external pen test and scan SKU (vPenTest-type tooling resells to providers) and a 'Safeguards testing' line item, reaching tax offices at near-zero CAC. The concept itself says its defence here is 'thin and relationship-based rather than a product moat'.
defensibility

The only thing automated tools lack is the founder's hands-on manual test and judgment. That is a services edge: it caps at about 40-60 clients, cannot be sold to an acquirer, and has no regulatory premium unless a manual test counts for more than an automated one under 314.4(d)(2), which the concept leaves open. If automated tests suffice, a cheaper automated rival can credibly claim the same compliance.
founder-fit

The paid core is now a founder-run annual penetration test, and the founder's testing record is CTFs plus PenTest+. There are no client engagements, references or sample reports. An MSP that resells the test under its own brand, an E&O/cyber insurer pricing a solo tester's cover, and an owner whose regulator may ask 'who tested you' will all want proof of earlier paid work. Without it the price is hard to defend and cover may cost more. This can be fixed: a few discounted or free scoped tests with written authorization and permission to use the client as a reference, plus a redacted sample report, before the paid launch.
founder-fit

The channel is now right for a technical founder: MSPs speak the founder's language and mortgage brokers buy all year. But it is still unbuilt. The founder has 'a few industry contacts', and the concept's own risks say MSPs may see a third party's findings on their tenants as grading their work. MSPs that already run compliance-as-a-service, such as ScalePad ControlMap priced per client per month, have a tool and may only want testing hours, not the whole Program. If no MSP signs, the plan falls back to one-to-one founder sales, which round 1 judged slow.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: Small financial offices above 5,000 consumers, or MSPs on their behalf, will pay about $2k/year for verified configuration and 314.4(d)(2) testing on top of the WISP and cyber insurance they already buy.
riskiest_assumption.test: In two weeks, without building software: offer 15 MSPs that serve accounting or mortgage offices a white-label pilot, and email 40 mortgage brokers and established tax offices a fixed-fee $490 'Safeguards testing check' (manual external scan plus a read-only M365 review delivered by hand). In 10 owner calls, ask about consumer count, insurer questionnaires and whether anyone has asked for proof of testing.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: At least 3 paid $490 checks or 1 MSP letter of intent covering 10+ client offices, and at least 4 of 10 owners above 5,000 consumers saying they have no annual test or vulnerability assessment and would pay to have one.

change_my_mind: market-skeptic
The concept's own test passes: at least 3 paid $490 checks or 1 MSP letter of intent covering 10+ offices within two weeks.
competitor-analyst
2-3 MSPs that serve accounting or mortgage offices and already own vPenTest, ConnectSecure or Cynomi sign a letter of intent to resell the Program, and say what they can't get from those tools.
security-practitioner

The monitor collects data daily and sends same-day alerts for external forwarding, new privileged roles and MFA removal; a 10-tenant pilot detects and contains at least one real or simulated BEC indicator within 24 hours.
technical-feasibility

A working prototype that onboards 3 real tenants (Business Basic, Standard and Premium) with one consent flow and returns MFA, forwarding and admin-role findings on each, with the Exchange role step timed and accepted
gtm-pricing
One signed MSP letter of intent covering 10+ client offices at the wholesale price, or at least 3 paid $490 testing checks from the 2-week test.
legal-ethics

A lawyer-reviewed engagement letter and test authorization template that requires the host's or MSP's written consent for any asset the office does not own, and an M365 test scope written to Microsoft's Rules of Engagement
economic-buyer

Cyber insurer or tax-pro/mortgage insurance programs ask for evidence of an annual test or vulnerability scans in renewal questionnaires, or discount premiums for it, so the spend moves into the insurance line.
defensibility

An exclusive or preferred referral agreement with a tax-pro or mortgage cyber-insurance program (e.g. PTIN.org's) or a state association that names this Program as accepted testing evidence for underwriting or premium credit.
founder-fit
The founder completes 3 scoped tests, at a discount if needed, that give written references and a redacted sample report, before May 2027.

name: QuietWin
one_liner: Verified Windows logging coverage for MSSPs on Wazuh: per-tenant audit-policy and Sysmon rollout, drift alerts and a monthly client evidence report.
entry_price: $9 per client tenant/month, minimum $149/month (e.g. $450/month at 50 tenants); onboarding $2,500 fixed, with a $500 single-tenant pilot credited toward it
majors: market-skeptic

There is still no buyer-side demand signal. All eight problem.evidence items come from in-house admins, a vendor blog or an enterprise survey, and most date from 2009-2021. The concept's own risks admit this. The new value claims (per-tenant drift alerts, a resellable client evidence report) have no evidence at all that any MSSP or SMB client asked for them.
market-skeptic

Narrowing the target makes the market smaller. The target is now MSSPs with 2-15 analysts that run their own Wazuh for Windows-heavy SMB clients and will not use Huntress, Blumira or LimaCharlie. That is a subset of a niche already estimated at low thousands. At $9 per tenant ($450/month at 50 tenants, about $5.4k/year), even 200 customers is roughly $1M ARR. The concept still gives no count. Its only route to scale is a Wazuh or RMM partner, and that is an open question.
market-skeptic

The forcing function is assumed, not shown. The pitch now depends on PCI DSS 10, HIPAA and cyber-insurance clients asking their MSSP for server logon evidence. The concept lists whether insurers or auditors actually ask for this as an open question. If they don't, the client report is a nice-to-have, and the MSSP cannot easily resell it per client.
competitor-analyst

The coverage verifier and drift alerts largely duplicate Wazuh Security Configuration Assessment (SCA). Wazuh ships CIS SCA policies that already run auditpol checks per agent, for example 'Audit Logon' Success and Failure, 'Audit Process Creation' and 'Audit Security Group Management'. Custom SCA YAML can check registry values (log sizes), running processes (Sysmon) and command output, and results show in the dashboard and alert when a check changes state. Per-tenant rollout of eventchannel collection and SCA policies is native through agent groups and agent.conf. An MSSP engineer can rebuild most of the 'stateful layer' with free features and no extra agent-side script, and Wazuh could ship a 'Windows logging coverage' SCA policy in a point release.
competitor-analyst

The concept says 'free Wazuh has no scheduled per-client evidence report', but the Wazuh 5.0 Reporting module supports scheduled and on-demand reports from saved dashboards, visualizations and searches, delivered by email under indexer RBAC. With a saved per-agent-group dashboard, a free monthly client PDF is a configuration task. The report runner's uniqueness shrinks to report content, such as logon and RDP narratives and coverage status, rather than the ability to produce and schedule a report.
competitor-analyst

Huntress remains the most dangerous channel competitor, with Wazuh close behind. Narrowing to MSSPs that 'keep their own Wazuh stack' avoids competing on volume, but it targets the segment that managed SIEMs bundling a SOC (Huntress, Blumira, LimaCharlie MSSP tiers) are pulling away. The addressable base shrinks while the product is being built, and the concept already calls it lifestyle-scale.
security-practitioner

The 'Lean' profile drops events in Wazuh agent eventchannel XPath queries, and the concept names Wazuh compressed archives as the full-fidelity safety net. Wazuh archives only hold events that the manager received, so events filtered at the agent never reach archives.json. The safety net does not cover the drops it is meant to back. An IR lead who reads the docs will catch this, and the drops stay unrecoverable. Real options: keep full collection and filter with manager-side rules (archive everything, alert on less), or keep a local full-size Windows log retention window on each host.
security-practitioner

The paid 'stateful layer' is a custom verifier pushed through RMM, but Wazuh already does this natively. SCA policies run scheduled per-agent command and registry checks (auditpol output, Sysmon service and config hash, EventLog MaxSize) and report pass/fail changes into Wazuh. Agent groups (agent.conf) push localfile/eventchannel config per tenant. A practitioner would rather run vendor-native SCA YAML than grant a solo vendor's signed scripts execution on 50 tenants through RMM. Rebuild the verifier as SCA policies plus group config, and keep RMM only for GPO and Sysmon install. That cuts both the trust burden and the 'Wazuh could add it' gap to a thin layer.
security-practitioner

Configuration state is not delivery. Correct auditpol and Sysmon settings still lose events when the agent's client buffer overflows, when EPS limits are hit, when channels are disabled, or when an agent goes silent. A monthly client report that says 'covered' on config checks alone gives false assurance, and that report is a liability for the MSSP. Drift checks need an end-to-end heartbeat: generate a known test event per channel on each host and alert when it does not land in the indexer.
technical-feasibility

Schedule is still optimistic. Thirteen weeks have to cover: 3-5 weeks learning Wazuh (the concept's own estimate); 4 role packs x Keep/Lean x standalone/built-in Sysmon; a verifier; decoders, rules and dashboards; a PDF report runner; signed RMM rollout with rings and rollback; compliance and DPIA templates; and a replay lab of ~20 techniques per role (~80 tests). Paid onboarding also starts in month one. A realistic figure is 4-5 months, or 3 months with the lab and Lean profiles deferred.
technical-feasibility

Wazuh indexes alerts, not events. Archives are off by default and need logall_json plus extra index storage before raw events can be searched. Per-event-ID volume and a complete logon/RDP/logoff report therefore only work in one of two ways. Either the packs ship rules that raise every 4624/4634/4778/4779/4672 event to an indexed alert level, which adds the indexer volume the product is meant to tame, or the MSSP indexes archives. Wazuh Cloud has no shell on the manager, so the runner can only use APIs. The concept doesn't choose between these designs.
gtm-pricing

Cancel-and-keep is still structural. The verifier, drift rules, dashboards and report runner all run inside the MSSP's environment with no hosted component or licence check, so after onboarding an MSSP can stop paying and keep drift alerts and monthly reports running. The subscription then sells only future updates and support, which change slowly (audit-policy and Sysmon schemas are stable).
gtm-pricing

The planned scalable channel is weak. Wazuh's partner program has Gold and Platinum tiers for resellers and MSSPs who pay Wazuh to join (search results put the first-year cost at about $3.2k-$9.9k). It offers Wazuh Cloud, multi-tenancy and listing as a certified service partner, not a marketplace for third-party content. Without it, distribution is founder-led community work into a niche of low-thousands firms.
gtm-pricing

The revenue ceiling is set by founder time. At $9/tenant and 20-60 tenants, a typical MSSP pays $149-$540/month (about $1.8k-$6.5k ARR) plus a one-off $2,500 onboarding the founder delivers personally. One person can probably run 1-2 onboardings a month alongside pack maintenance and the replay lab, so 12-month ARR is likely $50-100k. The concept already calls this lifestyle-scale.
legal-ethics

The product now issues client-facing evidence: a monthly PDF with 'coverage status' and per-pack PCI DSS 10 / HIPAA 164.312(b) mapping. MSSP clients will attach it to audit evidence or cyber-insurance questionnaires. If drift went undetected or the mapping is read as 'compliant', a misstatement to an insurer can jeopardise cover, and the claim chain runs MSSP to QuietWin. The lawyer-reviewed agreement with liability cap, no-completeness warranty and E&O cover is still listed as a need, not done, and the report needs explicit 'not a compliance attestation' wording and a stated verification time window.
economic-buyer

The new forcing function is weak. PCI DSS Req. 10 and HIPAA 164.312(b) require that audit logs exist and are reviewed. They don't require this product. Free Wazuh already ships regulatory-compliance tagging and dashboards (PCI DSS, HIPAA, GDPR, NIST) in its ruleset, so the compliance reason is claimed by what I already run. Most SMB card merchants are SAQ-level, and the HIPAA rule is non-prescriptive. No auditor finding or insurer clause yet makes me buy, and the insurer question is still open.
economic-buyer

The economics rest on reselling the report, which is untested. If clients won't pay a separate line for a 'monthly evidence report', the fee is pure cost and I expect monthly reporting to be part of the managed-security fee I already charge. The concept's own success signal (4 of 15 would resell) is an intention, not a price clients have accepted.
economic-buyer

Build versus buy. The named user is my own detection engineer. sysmon-modular and Yamato give the configs for free. A PowerShell verifier plus a few Wazuh rules and an indexer query for a PDF is a few weeks of in-house work that I own forever. At $9/tenant I'd pay only if the replay-tested maintenance and Sysmon-migration support clearly beat that one-off effort. I'd want the pilot to show hours saved per tenant.
economic-buyer

Vendor risk now sits on my clients' domain controllers. The product pushes auditpol, Sysmon and scripts via RMM from a one-person vendor with no SOC 2 or security attestation. My clients' vendor-risk questionnaires and my own E&O carrier will ask about that supply chain. Signed packs and staged rings help, but I'd need attestation-grade evidence and a code-review right before rollout to every client DC.
defensibility

Wazuh itself is the most likely copier, and it could ship this within a quarter. Its SCA module runs YAML policies with registry and command checks (for example auditpol output, the Sysmon service and log-size keys) and raises alerts whenever a check changes status. Its agent groups push one agent.conf per group to that group's agents. The 'coverage verifier + drift alert' is therefore one SCA policy plus group configs, and Wazuh already ships CIS-based Windows policies. A 'Windows logging coverage' policy would be a small release item.
defensibility

The stateful layer is still copyable files on the customer's side. The verifier, decoders, rules, dashboards and report runner all run inside the MSSP environment with no hosted service, so a customer can cancel and keep running the last version. A Wazuh partner or consultant can also repackage it for their own clients. The state (per-tenant drift history) lives in the MSSP's indexer, not with QuietWin.
defensibility

The only real moat named in the revision log, an opt-in cross-MSSP coverage benchmark, is missing from the MVP features and appears only as a hope in risks. Local-only tooling with no data leaving the MSSP makes it hard to build. Without it there are no data or network effects.
founder-fit

Scope is narrower but still heavy for one person in 3 months: 4 role packs x 2 Sysmon flavours x Keep/Lean profiles, a verifier deployed 'via RMM' without naming which RMM (NinjaOne, Datto, N-able, ConnectWise each need their own script packaging and test tenant), a PDF report runner against the Wazuh indexer, a ~20-technique replay CI lab, compliance mappings and DPIA templates, plus 3-5 weeks learning Wazuh decoders and dashboards. Realistic first sellable cut is 4-5 months unless v1 is DC + workstation packs, one RMM and a simple HTML report.
founder-fit

Credibility with MSSP owners is addressed only by plan, not proof: the founder still has no production SOC/MSSP history, and the concept itself budgets 3-6 months of public replay-tested work before trust. Combined with 3 months to MVP, realistic recurring revenue starts at month 6-9; until then income depends on $500 pilots and $2,500 onboardings closed from a few contacts.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: Small MSSPs on Wazuh will pay per client tenant for verified, monitored Windows coverage and a client evidence report, rather than deploying free configs themselves.
riskiest_assumption.test: Over two weeks, hold 15 short calls with Wazuh-running MSSPs from the founder's contacts and Wazuh/r/msp communities, showing a mock client evidence report and drift alert (slides, no product), asking what they use today and offering the $500 single-tenant pilot with payment up front.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: At least 6 of 15 say they tried free configs (sysmon-modular, Yamato, Wazuh defaults) and still lack per-tenant verification or client reports, at least 4 say they would resell the report per client, and at least 2 pay the $500 pilot.
